summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening & intake system requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review of state screening and responses

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Reversing a one-page order dismissing an abuse and neglect petition, the Court held that a circuit court that sees reasonable cause to believe additional abuse or neglect exists may compel DHHR to investigate and amend the petition, and must enter findings of fact and conclusions of law on the allegations.
key_cases.relevance: A court may not let the agency screen out or abandon allegations without findings.
key_cases.quote: the circuit court has the inherent authority to compel the Department to amend its petition to encompass the evidence or allegations

key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of Tiffany Marie S.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming a finding of abuse and neglect, the Court held that a circuit court's findings of fact in an abuse and neglect case may be disturbed only if clearly erroneous, while its conclusions of law are reviewed de novo, and that the Department must prove the conditions existing when the petition was filed by clear and convincing proof.
key_cases.relevance: A screen-out or unfounded conclusion challenged on appeal is reviewed under this deferential standard for factual determinations.
key_cases.quote: absent a mistake of law, an appellate tribunal should disturb a circuit court's determination only if it is clearly erroneous

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Vacating the adjudicatory and dispositional orders, the Court held that a Rule 26(a) stipulated adjudication must contain agreed facts supporting court involvement and a statement of the respondent's problems, and that without a proper adjudication the circuit court had no jurisdiction to proceed to disposition.
key_cases.relevance: An informal or undocumented resolution at the front of the case cannot substitute for adjudicatory findings.
key_cases.quote: Without properly made findings of abuse and/or neglect at adjudication, a case cannot proceed to disposition

key_cases.case_name: Martin v. Saint Mary's Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Affirming judgment for the social workers, the court held that conduct that was at most negligent in bringing about the children's removal cannot support a § 1983 claim, so the defendants were entitled to qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: Errors and miscommunications in agency handling are judged by more than negligence before liability attaches.
key_cases.quote: Because a § 1983 claim cannot be sustained, it follows that the defendants are entitled to qualified immunity

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Vacating the termination order and remanding, the Court held that a circuit court may not terminate parental rights without first adjudicating the parent as having abused or neglected the child, where the same court had expressly concluded three months earlier that the father had not abused or neglected them.
key_cases.relevance: An allegation the court has rejected cannot be carried forward into disposition; where the agency's theory of abuse or neglect fails, the case must end at adjudication rather than proceed on the agency's preference.
key_cases.quote: a circuit court may not terminate a parent's rights to his child without first finding that the parent abused or neglected his child

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Vacating both dispositional orders, the Court held that the fifteen-of-twenty-two-months filing trigger does not relieve the Department of presenting, or the circuit court of finding, affirmative evidence supporting termination, and that the court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over a child who did not meet the statutory definition of an abused or neglected child.
key_cases.relevance: It is the recent WV authority, relied on in In re Z.S., on what an adjudication must actually establish: a child safely placed with non-abusing legal guardians before the petition does not meet the statutory definition, and the case as to that child should never have gone forward.
key_cases.quote: Because B.S. was not an abused or neglected child, the circuit court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to address, and ultimately terminate, the petitioner's parental rights to this child
